Time is a fascinating

What is the Scientific and Philosophical Phenomenology behind the nature of time and it's rampant lossiness? From what I have researched briefly, we sense time by scale; and that scale is somewhat Logarithmic. For example, for a person of 20 years old, half of their life is 10 years. One year is essentially 5% of their total lifespan; proportionally less significant than someone of 10 years of age, whom by adding one year, is 10% of their total lifespan.

The variable of one year, in this case, is constant, yet the proportionality is drastically different. What's even more fascinating (perhaps, philosophically tragic) is how this proportion increasingly (logarithmically) diminishes the depth of time; every year a person celebrates their birthdate, one year holds less proportionality.

That is not to say "this year is less significant than the year prior becuase it was Logarithmically less significant." That is a materialistic philosophy; not what I am alluding to. I am, however, focusing on the problem of time perception, and how fast time seems to exhaust oneself; every year, time appears to increase in velocity, while decreasing in spacing. Eventually, a year passes by and a person may feel as it if vanished.

That is where memories, novelty, reason, meaning and the Philosophical Phenomenology are the next Domain of inquiry; When the Science reports the Mathematical Dynamics, what is one to do Philosophically?
